deck.title: System Safety Analysis Techniques Concept Cards

cards.backDefinition: A structured examination of a system's hazards, failure paths, controls, and risk contributors using qualitative or quantitative techniques to understand how unsafe outcomes can arise and how risk can be reduced.
cards.whyItMatters: System-level analysis helps reveal interactions and failure combinations that may be missed when hazards are considered only one component or task at a time.
cards.keyPoint: Choose analysis techniques that match the system, decision, complexity, and available information.

sourceRefs.locator: System Safety > hazard analysis, reliability calculations, and risk-management techniques

cards.backDefinition: A top-down, deductive logic technique that starts with a defined undesired top event and works backward through combinations of lower-level failures or conditions that can produce that event.
cards.whyItMatters: FTA makes combinations and dependencies visible, helping analysts identify critical failure paths and evaluate how multiple causes can combine to produce a hazardous outcome.
cards.keyPoint: FTA reasons from the unwanted outcome toward its possible causes.

sourceRefs.locator: NUREG-0492 - fault tree construction and evaluation

cards.backDefinition: The defined system failure or undesirable outcome placed at the top of a fault tree and explained by tracing the combinations of lower-level events that can lead to it.
cards.whyItMatters: A precise top event establishes the scope and boundary of the analysis. An ambiguous top event can produce an unfocused or incomplete fault tree.
cards.keyPoint: Define the top event clearly before decomposing its causes.

sourceRefs.locator: NUREG-0492 - fault tree construction and evaluation

cards.backDefinition: A smallest combination of basic events that is sufficient, under the modeled fault-tree logic, to cause the top event; removing any event from that combination means the combination is no longer sufficient.
cards.whyItMatters: Minimal cut sets expose the combinations that can defeat the system and provide a compact basis for identifying important contributors and quantifying top-event probability.
cards.keyPoint: A minimal cut set contains no unnecessary event for producing the modeled top event.

sourceRefs.locator: NUREG-0492 - fault tree evaluation and cut-set analysis

cards.backDefinition: A bottom-up, inductive technique that examines how individual items or functions can fail and traces the effects of each failure through higher levels of the system.
cards.whyItMatters: FMEA systematically exposes vulnerable components, failure propagation, detection needs, and opportunities for design or operational controls before failures occur in service.
cards.keyPoint: FMEA reasons from individual failure modes toward their consequences.

sourceRefs.locator: Software FMEA > bottom-up analysis and basic procedure

cards.backDefinition: A specific manner in which an item, function, component, or interface can fail to perform its intended function or can perform it incorrectly.
cards.whyItMatters: Identifying distinct failure modes prevents an FMEA from treating all failures as equivalent and supports more specific consequence, detection, and control analysis.
cards.keyPoint: Describe how the item fails, not only that it fails.

sourceRefs.locator: Software FMEA > identify potential item and interface failure modes

cards.backDefinition: The consequence produced by a failure mode at the local, next-higher, or overall system level within the defined scope of an FMEA.
cards.whyItMatters: Tracing effects shows whether a local failure remains contained, degrades a function, propagates to other parts of the system, or contributes to a hazardous state.
cards.keyPoint: Follow the failure far enough to understand its system-level consequence.

sourceRefs.locator: Software FMEA > evaluate each failure mode and its potential consequences

cards.backDefinition: A forward, branching analysis that begins with an initiating event and follows the success or failure of responding functions, systems, or actions to identify possible sequences and end states.
cards.whyItMatters: Event trees show how different responses after the same initiating event can lead to recovery or progressively more severe outcomes, making sequence-dependent risk visible.
cards.keyPoint: ETA moves forward from the initiating event through alternative response paths.

sourceRefs.locator: Probabilistic Risk Assessment > event trees model plant response to initiating events

cards.backDefinition: An event that challenges normal operation and starts the sequence analysis used to evaluate how systems and people respond and what outcomes can follow.
cards.whyItMatters: Defining the initiator establishes the starting condition for an event tree and helps ensure that subsequent branch probabilities and system responses are interpreted consistently.
cards.keyPoint: The initiating event starts the sequence; it is not the final consequence.

sourceRefs.locator: Probabilistic Risk Assessment > initiating event and accident sequences

cards.backDefinition: A path through an event tree representing a particular combination of system responses and operator actions following an initiating event, leading to a defined outcome or end state.
cards.whyItMatters: Sequence analysis separates different pathways to an outcome, allowing analysts to identify which combinations of failures or successes contribute most to overall risk.
cards.keyPoint: Each sequence is one modeled path from initiator to outcome.

sourceRefs.locator: Probabilistic Risk Assessment > accident sequences and event-tree paths

cards.backDefinition: A structured, documented demonstration that major accident hazards have been identified and that effective arrangements and controls are in place to manage the associated risks within the applicable regulatory regime.
cards.whyItMatters: The approach requires the dutyholder to assemble a coherent demonstration of risk control rather than relying on isolated studies or an unsupported statement that the system is safe.
cards.keyPoint: A safety case is a demonstration of how major-accident risk is controlled, not merely a list of hazards.

sourceRefs.locator: Offshore health and safety law > safety case demonstrates ability and means to control major accident risks

cards.backDefinition: Aggregation of risk contributions from defined accident sequences or scenarios to obtain a total risk measure for a common endpoint using consistent units, boundaries, and model assumptions.
cards.whyItMatters: A system can have many individually small contributors. Summation shows their combined importance and prevents decisions from focusing only on the single largest scenario.
cards.keyPoint: Only combine contributions that represent the same risk endpoint and compatible basis.

sourceRefs.locator: Probabilistic Risk Assessment > sequence frequencies summed to calculate total core damage frequency
